sections.title: Abstract
sections.tag: What is this paper's contribution in brief?
sections.text:
Abstract
Many communities, including the scientific community, develop
implicit writing norms. Understanding them is crucial for effective
communication with that community. Writers gradually develop an
implicit understanding of norms by reading papers and receiving
feedback on their writing. However, it is difficult to both externalize
this knowledge and apply it to one’s own writing. We propose two

CHI ’25, April 26–May 01, 2025, Yokohama, Japan
new writing support concepts that reify document and sentence-
level patterns in a given text corpus: (1) an ordered distribution over
section titles and (2) given the user’s draft and cursor location, many
retrieved contextually relevant sentences. Recurring words in the
latter are algorithmically highlighted to help users see any emergent
norms. Study results (N=16) show that participants revised the
structure and content using these concepts, gaining confidence in
aligning with or breaking norms after reviewing many examples.
These results demonstrate the value of reifying distributions over
other authors’ writing choices during the writing process.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.tag: Why do writers need support learning implicit norms?
sections.text:
1 Introduction
Inexperienced researchers often lack knowledge of the implicit
writing conventions and structural expectations of particular com-
munities. While existing writing guides offer general advice, they
are often too abstract and high-level, making it challenging for
junior researchers to apply this guidance in their own work.
Given that people commonly learn through examples, providing
access to relevant examples can help bridge this gap. However, there
are obstacles: viewing too few examples may lead to overfitting
and unintentional plagiarism, while viewing too many examples—
without sufficient cognitive supports within the interface—may
overwhelm the writer.
Prior work motivated the design of writing support tools with
social cognitive theories and cognitive apprenticeship theory [18,
19] to help writers learn complex writing skills in a professional
setting. While this approach allows novices to learn by mimicking
model examples, it also requires expert knowledge to create and
annotate these examples, which is often time-consuming and not
readily available for many communities.
Learning from examples has also been extensively covered in the
language learning literature. Non-native English speakers (NNES)
may hesitate to choose from AI-suggested content because they
struggle to evaluate the content’s fluency and naturalness [21, 24,
25]. To address this problem, researchers proposed that novices
learn by inspecting sentences from a curated corpus such as the
Corpus of Contemporary American English (COCA)1 or English
dictionaries [4] to help students learn the correct use of colloca-
tions and phrases [35]. To this end, LangSmith proposed a writing
support tool for drafting academic NLP papers [20] by generating
grammatically correct phrases given the user’s current draft along
1https://www.english-corpora.org – accessed 12.09.2024
Hai Dang, Chelse Swoopes, Daniel Buschek, and Elena L. Glassman
with prior section and paper titles. In contrast, our work surfaces ex-
isting text from a relevant peer-reviewed text corpus. Furthermore,
by avoiding automatically generated text that may—without the
writer’s knowledge—cross the line into plagiarism if used verbatim,
the writer only sees previously published example sentences and
their provenance, retaining informed control.
To this end, we implemented CorpusStudio, a writing environ-
ment with two novel writing support concepts, one at the document
level and one at the sentence level, that help writers learn about
the writing styles and expectations of particular audiences. These
writing supports are designed to expose writers to as many ex-
amples as possible to increase the variety of examples shown to
the users—with the cognitive support necessary to help them see
the emergent patterns that capture otherwise implicit community-
specific writing content and style expectations. Specifically, at the
document level, CorpusStudio computes and renders an ordered dis-
tribution [15] over section title sequences in prior papers from the
community the writer wishes to write for. This gives the writer a
sense of common and uncommon section titles and in what relative
order they appear in prior papers (Figure 1A). At the sentence level,
CorpusStudio retrieves many example sentences from the corpus
given the user’s draft-in-progress and their current cursor location
within it (Figure 1C). Words across these many example sentences
are algorithmically highlighted or de-emphasized to help users see
any emergent norms and outliers. We also allow authors to capture
their thoughts and deductions from viewing these examples with
bookmarks and notes.
We conducted a user study with N=16 participants from the
academic community who were actively writing their manuscripts.
They used CorpusStudio to draft their paper outline, wrote one
to two sections of their manuscript, and answered questionnaires
eliciting their overall experience writing within CorpusStudio.
Our results reveal that users felt more confident in their writing
when they discovered that other people in their target community
have written in a similar way. Inspecting many examples at once
was useful for identifying broad structural patterns, especially for
sections that typically have more common structure, such as the
description of the system implementation details or participants’
demographics.
In summary, we contribute the following:
•
We designed two novel writing support concepts that make
visibleemergentpatternsatthe document-leveland sentence-
level of a given paper corpus.
•
We implemented these writing support concepts within Cor-
pusStudio, an interactive writing environment that helps
writers retrieve, inspect, generalize from, and reflect on many
examples from their target venue
• We found that users’ writing goals guided their perception
of relevance and how they adapted content from the corpus.

sections.title: 2 Background and Related Work
sections.tag: How does prior work address writing norms and examples?
sections.text:
2 Background and Related Work
In this section we provide a background on writing norms in differ-
ent communities and how members learn about these norms. We
then give an overview of interactive tools that support writing and
tools for finding related work.

CorpusStudio: Surfacing Emergent Patterns in a Corpus of Prior Work while Writing
2.1 Community Writing Norms
Flower [12]
2.1.1 The Importance of Understanding Writing Norms.
highlights the difference between writer-based and reader-based
prose, arguing that the former represents the writers’ unrefined
thoughts while the latter requires their careful transformation with
the reader goals in mind while ensuring a shared language and
shared context. Prior writing literature emphasizes the importance
of writing for an audience [1, 16, 45], but writing for academic
or professional communities can be especially difficult because
they have implicit writing expectations and failing to address them
may confuse its members or waste their time with “unfocused and
pointless discussions” [12].
2.1.2 Aspects of Writing Norms. Writing norms are comprised of
many aspects, including the language, content, organization of
information, and scope of the written document. Although aca-
demic venues may provide a high-level overview of the expected
content and style of writing such as encouraging authors to write
“clearly and concisely, avoid jargon, organize the submission to
detail”2,
flow logically and smoothly, provide the right level of it
can be challenging for novice writers to apply these suggestions in
their own writing, e.g., What is the expected level of detail for that
audience?
2.1.3 Learning about a Community’s Writing Norms. To support
writing in an academic context, prior research has proposed the
cognitive apprenticeship theoretic approach to teach novices com-
plex cognitive tasks by mimicking experienced members of the
community [8]. Drawing from these ideas, our work instantiates
two strategies of cognitive apprenticeship, namely modeling and
reflection.
2.2 Writing with External Text
2.2.1 Writing with Retrieved or Generated Additional Text. Many
writing support tools facilitate writing by suggesting content that
users did not write themselves. Sentence completions are a frequent
form of writing assistance [2, 28]. However, direct content genera-
tion can have negative impacts such as diminishing the author’s self-
expression and ownership over the final text outcome [30]. Related
work has also looked into providing writing inspirations [6, 14, 43].
We build on this line of research by surfacing prior text as the
user writes new text (e.g., Naeem et al. [37] and IntroAssist [18]). A
critical difference is the much larger scale of prior text surfaced to
the user and post-processed for emergent patterns in our work. For
example, IntroAssist [18] presents expert-curated email examples to
help users draft their help-seeking message in a professional con-
text, while our approach uses computational methods to show many
examples drawn from a large text corpus of previously published
papers.
2.2.2 Writing with Text from a Corpus. Hui and Sprouse [19] pro-
posed a writing support tool to help college students write in a
professional context assisted by scaffolded annotations. The authors
proposed a checklist with multiple annotations that provide cues
about the content to include in the professional email. This checklist
2https://chi2025.acm.org/submission-guides/guide-to-a-successful-submission/ – ac-
cessed: 31 January 2025
CHI ’25, April 26–May 01, 2025, Yokohama, Japan
is complemented with model texts where sections of that text have
been annotated with the elements of the checklist. This approach
helps users understand the overall structure and expected content
while also demonstrating concrete instantiations of the high-level
guidelines. Our concepts help users plan the structure and content
of their writing by showing many concrete examples of how other
members of their target community have written similar texts.
2.3 Finding Relevant Examples
As previously described, writers learn from inspecting examples,
but finding related work with the purpose of writing support is chal-
lenging. Search engines such as Google Scholar, the ACM Digital
Library, Mendeley, and Semantic Scholar typically surface docu-
ments based on topical similarity while writers need specific analo-
gous snippets of text from the manuscript to inform their writing.
Current tools also help researchers understand how their own
work relates to other work [29] by contextualizing embedded cita-
tions [5], drawing connections to follow-on work directly in the
paper document [40], and making recommendations based on a
paper’s metadata such as citations and authorship [7, 23, 39, 42] or
its semantic similarity [3, 17, 23]. In contrast, our design focuses on
finding related work for the purpose of writing support, i.e., that
helps writers identify existing writing conventions from a specific
community.
Most interactive research tools either support analyzing related
work [26, 29, 33, 38] or writing with computational help [9, 28]. In
existing contexts, writers often need to navigate away from their
writing environment to search for related work, scroll through the
target document, select and process relevant text structures and
draw conclusions about the implicit writing conventions encoded
in the target document. Performing all of these steps leads to abrupt
context switches and breaks the writing flow. Our approach pro-
poses an integrated environment to support writing and searching
for model text in the same interface, thereby minimizing the num-
ber of context switches and streamlining the writing and research
process.

sections.title: 3 Corpus Studio
sections.tag: What is CorpusStudio and how is it designed?
sections.text:
3 Corpus Studio
We designed CorpusStudio to support writers in learning about
and applying community-specific writing norms. This is achieved
primarily through novel mechanisms for the retrieval and rendering
of content from a corpus of existing documents written by and for
that community.
3.1 Design Goals
Our overarching design goal is to empower users with evidence of
community-specific emergent norms and outliers at the document
and sentence level as they write their own document for the same
audience. In the process of fulfilling this overarching goal, our goal
is to reduce, not facilitate, unintentional human- or AI-generated
plagiarism.
3.2 Usage Scenario
Alice has been working on a new interactive writing support system
and is drafting her manuscript for submission to an HCI venue. She
has some prior experience writing academic papers but is unfamiliar

CHI ’25, April 26–May 01, 2025, Yokohama, Japan
with writing papers with a focus on a system contribution. She
opens CorpusStudio to learn more about her target venue’s writing
expectations while working on her draft.
Inspecting the section titles. She looks at the ordered distribution
over section titles. As shown in Figure 1A, she expands the cluster
named Implementation, which typically comes after System Design
and around the same location as Methods (when those sections
exist in a given paper). In the expanded cluster, she observes how
other authors have phrased this typical section’s title, i.e., more
commonly Implementation and less commonly Implementation De-
tails or Implementation of <System Name>. Although she likes the
idea of adding a system name to the title, she decides to stick with
the more generic commonly chosen option for now, and finishes
her paper outline of section titles in the text editor beside it.
Inspecting the retrieved sentences. In the text editor, she starts
drafting the implementation section immediately under the Im-
plementation section title, but she does not know how she should
introduce it. She writes a few words and, without moving the cursor,
hits the TAB key to retrieve related sentences from other work to
get a sense of what (and how) other people wrote the beginnings of
their implementation sections. She notices that many authors start
with “We implemented <name of the system> to do/test <some
hypothesis>” while some also state their design rationale.
Developing a personal style sheet. She bookmarks one of the re-
trieved sentences to remind herself of this observation and adds the
note: “The first paragraph of the implementation is often formulaic
and with this recognizable structure.” She concludes that it is prob-
ably well accepted in the community if she starts her paragraph in
a similar way.
Continuing Writing. Alice continues to write down her ideas in
the text editor and occasionally retrieves example sentences given Introduction is the ubiquitous starting
where her cursor is when she needs inspiration or wants to confirm
how other authors have written their manuscripts.
3.3 System Characteristics
In this work, the evidence of community-specific emergent norms
and outliers at both the document and sentence level is provided
to writers in the form of extracted examples from a corpus of doc-
uments written for and by their intended audience. To facilitate
the writer’s recognition of these emergent norms from examples
without facilitating the writer’s anchoring on any one example too
much, we look to theories of human concept learning:
Variation Theory. Regardless of whether a human or a machine
is learning from examples, any learning process can fall victim to
overfitting, i.e., learn a rule that does not generalize to the rest of the
corpus, when trained on too little data. For example, the Variation
Theory of Learning [32] was explicitly designed to minimize human
overfitting when learning from examples. With only a few examples
or suggestions, previous systems may cause users to anchor [46] on
just one of them. By instead showing many examples, we hope the
user may be (1) less likely to anchor to one of the retrieved examples
(or even unintentionally plagiarize from it) and (2) more likely
to observe community writing norms and possibilities without
overfitting to the retrieved examples.
Hai Dang, Chelse Swoopes, Daniel Buschek, and Elena L. Glassman
Structural Alignment Theory. While the many retrieved examples
in our work are not algorithmically selected on the basis of Variation
Theory, the textual examples are ordered and rendered with visual
attributes (e.g., grayed-out repeated words or color-coordinated
highlights) designed to support the recognition of emergent com-
monalities and outliers, based on the human cognitive processes of
pattern recognition described by Structural Alignment Theory [13].
3.3.1 Text Editor. Users outline their paper and draft their prose
in the central text editor (Figure 1B). The editor supports two text
cell types: section title and paragraph.
Borrowing from the syntax of Markdown editors, the editor
allows users to create section titles by pre-pending text with #’s
where the number of #’s indicate the level of the section title.
3.3.2 Surfacing Document-levelCommunity-specificEmergentNorms
and Outliers. Inspecting outlines from other papers in the target
community can help writers develop their own. To help writers un-
derstand how papers are commonly (and uncommonly) structured
within their target community at the document level, we show an
ordered distribution of section title clusters from the entire corpus
immediately to the left of the central text editor (Figure 1A Section
Titles From Other Papers). This ordered distribution is computed by
applying Positional Diction Clustering (PDC) [15] to the ordered
lists of top-level section titles extracted from each paper in the
corpus.
PDC is a structural mapping engine [11] designed to algorith-
mically emulate at scale the analogical matching process humans
do when comparing two or more structurally similar objects, as de-
scribed by Structural Alignment Theory [13]. In CorpusStudio, the
objects are papers, and the resulting order of section title clusters
that PDC generates preserves the section titles’ approximate rela-
tive positions in their respective papers. For example, in Figure 1A,

CorpusStudio: Surfacing Emergent Patterns in a Corpus of Prior Work while Writing
3.3.3 Surfacing Sentence-level Community-specific Emergent Norms
and Outliers. This writing support is intended to provide insights
into both established conventions and areas where variation is
common at the sentence level. By retrieving and displaying many
relevant sentences simultaneously, users can observe how similar
content is expressed across different papers. These distributions can
reveal both rigid conventions (narrow distributions) and areas of
flexibility (wide distributions). For instance, participant descriptions
in user studies often follow stereotypical patterns, while discus-
sion sections typically show more variation to accommodate novel
findings.
Spatial Retrieval. At the core of our approach is a novel retrieval
mechanism we call analogous spatial retrieval, which integrates
context, content, and spatial information. Users can request this
retrieval of sentences from other papers by hitting the TAB key
as they are drafting their text. Given where the user’s cursor is
placed in the text editor at the moment of retrieval (i.e., the text
of the currently focused paragraph cell and the title of the section
containing it), we retrieve and display many potentially analogous
sentences from similarly titled sections of papers in the corpus
(Figure 1C What others wrote column) as well as the subsequent
sentence in each paper (Figure 1C What they wrote next column). See
Section 3.4 and Section 4.2 for more spatial retrieval implementation
details.
To further help writers “peek into the future,” that is, explore
what other authors wrote later in a given section, users can insert
empty paragraph cells after a non-empty paragraph cell and then
trigger sentence retrieval. The number of empty cells corresponds
to the offset o (in sentences) to be retrieved from the corpus. Retriev-
ing content with an offset works by first retrieving all sentences
that would have been retrieved if the cursor had been in the near-
est preceding non-empty paragraph cell but then retrieving and
displaying the o-th subsequent sentences.
Scale of Retrieval. Following Gentner’s work on analogical learn-
ing theory [13], the comparison of many example sentences pro-
motes the extraction of common principles or abstract schemas,
which may be more likely to be transferred to future writing tasks.
We experimented with displaying 10, 25 and 50 sentences at once
and found that 25 sentences provided enough content for writers to
explore and potentially recognize common principles and abstract
schemas while not overwhelming them.
Sentence Rendering. However, what writers learn from these
examples depends not only on their scale and variety, but also on
how the writer mentally processes and compares them [13]. To aid
in this mental sentence comparison process, the sentence examples
can be rendered with algorithmically assigned visual variables (e.g.,
color-coordinated highlights) designed to support the recognition
of emergent commonalities and outliers (and possibly support the
mental cross-sentence alignment process necessary for developing
abstract sentence schemas). Figure 2 shows a comparison of the
two available but optional rendering modes:
•

Re-ranking is another way for users to explore relationships

words to account for the new sorted column.
3.3.4 User Notes. As shown in Figure 3 and the top right callout
in Figure 1C, users can bookmark a sentence and then comment
on it in the User Notes section, e.g., with a reminder of why it
fulfills its purpose particularly well or poorly. These annotated
sentence examples can be exported as a csv file to facilitate sharing
observations, preferences, and insights with others.

CHI ’25, April 26–May 01, 2025, Yokohama, Japan
3.3.5 Contextual Tooltips. Writers may want to know more of the
context surrounding a retrieved sentence, e.g., to avoid misinter-
preting it. As shown in Figure 1D, users can hover over a retrieved
sentence to view a floating window showing the paper’s title, the
hierarchical section title path, and the sentences immediately before
and after. The paper title links to the full paper in the ACM Digital
Library. Additionally, if any retrieved sentence includes a citation,
users can hover over it to display the full citation information,
including the authors and the referenced paper title.
3.3.6 Features for Promoting Learning, not Plagiarism. A combina-
tion of features are intended to work together to support users in
actively engaging with many examples, rather than anchoring on
and copying any one. More specifically, showing multiple examples
at once may help novice writers make more informed decisions
about plagiarism: when sentences are highly similar across papers,
this often indicates accepted community writing norms (like in
methodology sections), while sections with more varied writing
styles suggest areas where similar phrasing should be avoided.
In concert with showing many examples, two additional design
choices are intended to further facilitate learning over plagiarism:
First, we disable the user’s ability to copy and paste retrieved sen-
tences into their own draft. Second, by providing visible affordances
for saving and annotating their insights, we may promote deeper
reflection on the writing patterns they observe.
3.4 Implementation Details
SvelteKit.4
We implemented our system as a web application using
WeaviateDB5
For sentence retrieval, we used as our vector database,
using its built-in text embedding capabilities and approximate k-
Nearest Neighbor (kNN) search implementation [34]. The system
was deployed on a workstation with 12 GB of GPU memory and
made remotely accessible to study participants.
While determining relevance in retrieval systems is inherently
complex and depends on users’ dynamic writing objectives, query-
ing based on semantic similarity in text vector space is an estab-
lished approach in retrieval-based systems [47]. Our initial im-
plementation explored hybrid search techniques, following prior
work that used Reciprocal Rank Fusion [41] to combine keyword-
based and vector-based retrieval results. However, through initial
experiments, we found pure vector-based search provided more
contextually relevant matches.

sections.title: 4 Data & Processing
sections.tag: How was the paper corpus collected and processed?
sections.text:
4 Data & Processing
We collected 478 papers from two HCI venues (IUI and UIST) which
included the proceedings from 2021 until 2023. These venues typ-
ically publish HCI system contributions. We completed the data
request process with the ACM.
4.1 Pre-processing Documents
We initially used the NLTK module to split each manuscript into
sentences, but we experienced many edge cases where extracted
sentences were incomplete. We therefore chose an LLM-based ap-
proach instructing the model to separate sentences by inserting
4https://kit.svelte.dev
5https://weaviate.io
Hai Dang, Chelse Swoopes, Daniel Buschek, and Elena L. Glassman
[EOS] tokens between sentences. For each extracted sentence, meta-
data was also saved, e.g., the context shown in the tooltips described
in Section 3.3.5.
4.2 Embedding Process
To implement spatial retrieval, we follow an approach resembling
LangSmith [20]. We prepared our corpus to support this function-
ality by pre-pending section titles to the extracted sentences be-
fore embedding the concatenated sequence using OpenAI’s ‘text-
embedding-small-3‘ model (Figure 4). This approach enables Cor-
pusStudio to retrieve related sentences based on both the section
title and the content of the sentence. We used default parameter
values and default un-trimmed vector dimensions.
4.3 Extracting an Ordered Distribution over
Section Titles
The sequences of top-level section titles for each paper were ex-
tracted and organized into a list of lists using positional diction
clustering (PDC) [15]. This is identical to the process that produced
the data for the Interleaved PDC view in Gero et al. [15], except
instead of processing LLM responses as sequences of sentences,
we processed papers as sequences of section titles. We also com-
puted how many papers had each section title in order to populate
a corresponding histogram in the CorpusStudio interface.
We experimented with different sample sizes ranging from 200,
500, 1000, to 5000 section titles and found that distinctive distribu-
tion characteristics quickly emerged even with smaller sample sizes.
For our prototype we decided to render and cluster 1000 section
titles to demonstrate both the defining characteristics of the section
title distribution while still providing a variety of ways authors
have organized and phrased their section titles.

sections.title: 5 User Study
sections.tag: How was CorpusStudio evaluated with users?
sections.text:
5 User Study
To evaluate our two novel writing support concepts (described
at the document level in Section 3.3.2 and at the sentence level
in Section 3.3.3), we used CorpusStudio to conduct a controlled
within-subjects experiment with participants who were, with one
exception, actively working towards writing a manuscript for an
HCI venue. Participants completed two writing tasks during the
user study: (i) drafting or revising an outline of their paper and (ii)
drafting or revising section(s) of their paper. We referred to Cor-
pusStudio as a “set of design features” or “prototype” during our
user evaluation of the concepts. We used Google Docs as our base-
line interface because it is a commonly used writing environment
in this context. We aimed to investigate how participants would
use the writing supports to achieve their goals, how the supports
would affect their writing process, and how they may help them
identify norms of a target community.
5.1 Participants
Sixteen participants were recruited through mailing lists and Slack
channels from different universities in the USA, Germany, United
Kingdom and South Korea (Table 1). Participants had most com-
monly authored or co-authored 3-5 academic papers already, but
two had authored less and four had authored more than twenty
(see Appendix Figure 12 for the entire distribution). The average

5.2 Study Procedure
All studies were conducted remotely via Zoom and were evenly
facilitated between the two lead co-authors. CorpusStudio was
accessible as a web application, so participants were not required to
install anything. Each study took approximately 60-75 minutes, and
participants received $25 (USD) via digital payment (Zelle, Venmo,
or PayPal) as compensation for their time.
5.2.1 Consent & Pre-Study Survey. Each participant, after giving
informed consent, completed a brief survey about their demograph-
ics, experience with scientific communication and writing for a
target venue, current strategies for writing, use and experience
with writing support tools, and questions relevant to the task that
they would be completing. All survey questions are included in
Appendix A.
5.2.2 Task Preparation. ParticipantswereinformedthatCorpusStu-
dio’s corpus, from which they would be viewing section titles and
retrieved sentences, consisted of papers from two HCI venues, IUI
and UIST, between 2021 and 2023. This information was disclosed to
ensure participants had a clear understanding of the corpus context,
allowing them to engage with the examples accordingly, regardless
of their own specific target venue.
Before starting each of the two tasks, participants watched a
tutorial video that explained the relevant writing support concept
and its supporting features in CorpusStudio. Participants were told
that we evaluated the features, not their work.
5.2.3 Task 1: Outline Writing. We chose outlining as our first task
because it let us examine how participants structured their work af-
ter seeing an ordered distribution over section titles from published
papers.
The outlining task had two sub-tasks: drafting section titles for
the first and second half of the paper. Participants used either a
baseline interface (Google Docs) or the exploratory interface (Cor-
pusStudio) in counterbalanced order. With the baseline, participants
relied on their typical resources. With CorpusStudio, they just used

CHI ’25, April 26–May 01, 2025, Yokohama, Japan
the Figure 1A Section Titles From Other Papers feature. Each sub-
task had a 5-minute limit. They thought aloud while writing and
completed post-task surveys (Appendix A.2, Appendix A.3).
5.2.4 Task 2: Paper Writing. Participants began writing or revising
sections of their manuscript for their target venue. They were given
the option to bring the outline created in the previous task and any
supporting text that they may have already written into this task.
Participants were allowed to use any feature of CorpusStudio to
help them write. As part of the task, participants were asked to
bookmark example sentences that they would want to save and
annotate in User Notes for themselves or a mentee. They were given
twenty minutes to complete the writing portion and five minutes
at the end to revise and update their User Notes; they also were
asked to think aloud while completing this task.
Note that, in the tutorial video at the beginning of the task,
we included the information about plagiarism and patterns over
retrieved sentences described in Section 3.3.6. We also provided the
following instruction: “When there is high diversity of sentence
content and style, read many sentences before composing your
thoughts to avoid mirroring any one sentence directly; this will
hopefully help you avoid plagiarism and ensure your work remains
authentic.”
5.2.5 Post-Tasks Survey and Interview. To conclude the task and
study, participants completed a post-task survey (see Appendix A.4)
followed by a brief semi-structured interview (see Appendix A.5).

Overview. Participants reported that seeing retrieved sentences
and section titles helped them overcome the blank page problem
and continue drafting. They also found it helpful to view multiple
contextually relevant sentences from various papers on a single
page within a centralized writing environment, which allowed for
easier comparison of structure and patterns. They reported that this

methods, such as having multiple papers open to compare texts.

tasks such as drafting introductions, starting sections, describing

We analyzed participants’ responses to survey questions using a
non-parametric Mann-Whitney U test. For Task 1, i.e., outline writ-

7.1 Task 1: Outline Writing
7.1.1 Usefulness of Drafting Tools. Participants rated the useful-

drafting it in CorpusStudio (Figure 6). Results indicated a statisti-

better structure for their outline, learning how to write for a new
venue or topic, and confirming their existing titles.
7.1.2 Ease of Drafting Section Title Outlines and Venue Alignment.
For both conditions, participants answered a series of questions
focusing on how easily they drafted section titles that were relevant
to their work, aligned with the style of the target venue, adhered
to norms, included all desired aspects, and identified when others
had broken norms. The average responses for each condition are
shown in Figure 7. A Mann-Whitney U test revealed no statistically
significant differences between the interface conditions for any of
these five Likert items.
7.1.3 Differences Between Tasks. Between the sub-tasks, i.e., draft-
ing the first half of the document compared to the second half, there
was a statistically significant difference (p=0.014) in participants’
responses to the question, “It was easy to create the section title
structure that my target venue expects.” This suggests potential
learning effects as participants found it easier to create the section
title structure in the second half. Participants could have adapted
their writing strategies from drafting the first half to the second
half. We found no significant differences in the other questions
within this category (see Appendix A.3.2 for the full questions).
We also evaluated whether different interface conditions im-
pacted the ease of drafting section titles and aligning them with
the target venue’s expectations for both the first and second halves
of the outline. Although no significant differences were found, our
qualitative findings suggest that participants had greater confidence
in their writing when using CorpusStudio due to the availability of
examples, which helped reduce uncertainty.

the 16 participants (87.5%) reported that writing the section titles
in CorpusStudio with Section Titles of Other Papers made the task
easier (via alleviating the blank page problem and having examples
at hand in a centralized writing environment), while the remaining
two participants reported that writing in the baseline interface was
easier.

tion titles in CorpusStudio felt more overwhelming because they
had to mentally process the distribution of section titles—yet most
acknowledged that, despite the initial challenge, the process was
useful for generating ideas. The remaining seven participants (44%)
reported that completing the task in the baseline interface felt more
overwhelming because they had to begin from an empty page and

was least frequently used. Some participants did not find it useful
to de-emphasize words, while others did not notice the feature at
all (Section 6.2.6). There was an overall positive sentiment on the
usefulness of all other features (Figure 10).
Eight of 16 participants (50%) answered that they had a clearer
sense of when it was appropriate to break the writing expectations
of the target venue after interacting with CorpusStudio while four
did not think that their understanding had changed and four gave
a neutral response (Figure 11). From the study, we observed that at
least three people commented on deviations between their prior as-
sumptions about the structure or content and the retrieved content
(Section 6.1).
All but two participants found that evaluating many sentences
from previous papers gave them a better understanding of the
typical writing expectations of the target venue (Figure 11). This
aligns with the qualitative results where participants commented
positively about the usefulness of inspecting retrieved sentences,
which gave them more confidence in their writing.

8.1 Relevance of Retrieved Sentences
We found that relevance of retrieved sentences was tightly coupled
with users’ writing intentions, as they found different uses and
rationales for integrating the retrieved results into their writing
process.
8.1.1 Users’ Diverse Applications of Retrieved Sentences. While Cor-
pusStudio uses text embeddings to capture semantic and syntactic
relationships [36], our study revealed that relevance was also deter-
mined by participants’ writing goals rather than semantic similarity
alone. For instance, semantically similar sentences were sometimes
less useful than structurally similar ones when writers sought to
understand the organization of the paper.
Participants sought inspiration at multiple levels of writing: from
paper organization through section titles to section-level transitions
and standard academic phrases. The writers shaped these results
through queries using their draft text itself, similar to patterns ob-
served in interactions with AI in writing [10]. This challenges funda-
mental information retrieval assumptions about query-document
similarity as an (only) indicator of relevance. While it provided
a useful starting point, our findings suggest that relevance of re-
trieved text in writing support systems is not fixed, but dynamically
constructed based on writers’ immediate goals.
8.1.2 Interpreting Retrieved Results: User Behaviors and Dataset
Limitations. Our study revealed how retrieved examples influenced
participants’ writing in unexpected ways. When participants were
looking for something specific and did not find it in the retrieved
results, this led to two notable behaviors: First, participants often
rephrased their text to get different results, blurring the line be-
tween writing and querying. Second, some interpreted a lack of
results as evidence of their work’s novelty, a problematic conclusion
given CorpusStudio’s limited scope (two HCI venues: IUI and UIST
from 2021-2023). These findings suggest that writing support sys-
tems should actively communicate their scope and limitations, for
instance by suggesting broader venue searches when topic-specific
queries yield no results, helping writers make informed decisions
about how to interpret search results.

8.2 Designing a System with Many Retrieved
Examples
While many writing support systems prioritize simplicity through
aggregatedresults,wedeliberatelypresentedmanyexamples(N=25)
to increase the variety of examples users saw. To help users process
the larger scale of information, we provided sentence rendering
modes that modulate visual variables of the text in a way intended
to support users in recognizing cross-sentence relationships. While
it provided support, it did not eliminate all the additional cognitive
demands of the extra information.
The study results suggest that showing multiple examples at
once is valuable despite its cognitive demands: seeing variations in
how similar ideas were expressed helped participants distinguish
between rigid conventions and flexible patterns in academic writ-
ing. This suggests a trade-off between cognitive load and learning
potential, a consideration for future writing support systems that
aim to support learning rather than just text production.
Given that readers have different visual preferences, we provided
more than one method for cognitive support. We encourage design-
ers who wish to show multiple parallel examples to also provide
alternate ways to help users visually identify patterns.
8.3 Designing Writing Support for and with
Community Integration, not AI Integration
Our concept provides relevant text snippets to support writing
but it does not use any AI-generated text, in contrast to recent
trends in writing assistant systems [27]. Instead of training AI on a
corpus, we surface examples from the corpus directly. In our case,
these examples can be assumed to meet the community’s quality
standards, because they are evaluated by its members beforehand,
that is, the published papers in the corpus went through peer review.
We argue that this approach values and supports communities.
For example, it might aid communities in discovering their own
community-level patterns of expression and in “onboarding” new
community members. Supporting this, our design includes func-
tionality for taking one’s own notes, which might later contribute
to exchanges between community members about writing norms,
i.e., beyond individual interactions with our system.

This approach may also make a community’s past work more
discoverable to its members. Our retrieval method is based on the
local text in the draft, and not on other metrics, such as paper
citation counts or author metrics. In this way, our concept might
contribute to discovering less well known but relevant work that the
writer would not have noticed otherwise. This could be examined
in a dedicated future study, and the UI design could be developed
further in this direction.
8.4 Putting Metacognitive Strategies “Ready to
Hand”
Tankelevitch et al. [44] recently motivated designing for metacog-
nitive challenges in interaction. One emerging approach here is to
do so by embedding specific thinking strategies directly into the
interface. For instance, Dang et al. [9] designed for the strategy
of “reverse outlining” by providing a sidebar of paragraph-wise
summaries, updated live. Similarly, we designed for learning from
examples, with respective material provided in sidebars directly
within the writing environment. Our design also supports the ex-
ternalization of users’ self-reflection (e.g., what does this mean for
my text?) in User Notes. As our results show, participants found
this helpful and made use of it in diverse ways.
Tankelevitch et al. [44] also suggests “support[ing] users in in-
creasing their self-awareness and adjusting their confidence.” We
observed that, by becoming aware of what authors in a community
wrote, many participants’ confidence levels increased with respect
to writing for that same community.
8.5 Limitations and Future Work
Our results reveal how writers interact with and perceive examples
retrieved from a community-specific document corpus. However,
readers should be cautious when generalizing these findings be-
yond the scope of our study. All participants had a background in
HCI, and the corpus was drawn from two HCI venues, focusing
primarily on system contribution papers. Additionally, the writing
task was based on an academic writing scenario. Future research
should explore other writing contexts where communities play a
role, such as fiction, poetry, or argumentative writing. In our user
study, participants were given 20-25 minutes to draft their text and
engage with the various system features. While this offered valu-
able insights into their interactions and perceptions of the writing
environment, it would be worthwhile to explore how prolonged use
of these features might influence users’ writing habits and style.
9 Conclusion
CorpusStudio is a writing support system that integrates example
retrieval—at both the document level and sentence level—directly
into the drafting process. Writers can compare their text against a
curated corpus from their target academic community, with the sys-
tem presenting many real examples in parallel. This tight coupling
between writing and retrieval enables authors to identify estab-
lished writing patterns, understand community conventions, and
validate their writing choices through direct comparison with pub-
lished work. Unlike systems that generate or remix text, CorpusStu-
dio deliberately preserves and attributes original manuscripts, using

aims to advance an interaction model where writing support tools

paragraphs.tag: What problem motivates this work and what was built and found?
paragraphs.text:
Many communities, including the scientific community, develop
implicit writing norms. Understanding them is crucial for effective
communication with that community. Writers gradually develop an
implicit understanding of norms by reading papers and receiving
feedback on their writing. However, it is difficult to both externalize
this knowledge and apply it to one’s own writing. We propose two

CHI ’25, April 26–May 01, 2025, Yokohama, Japan
new writing support concepts that reify document and sentence-
level patterns in a given text corpus: (1) an ordered distribution over
section titles and (2) given the user’s draft and cursor location, many
retrieved contextually relevant sentences. Recurring words in the
latter are algorithmically highlighted to help users see any emergent
norms. Study results (N=16) show that participants revised the
structure and content using these concepts, gaining confidence in
aligning with or breaking norms after reviewing many examples.
These results demonstrate the value of reifying distributions over
other authors’ writing choices during the writing process.

paragraphs.tag: Why is it hard for junior researchers to learn writing conventions?
paragraphs.text:
Inexperienced researchers often lack knowledge of the implicit
writing conventions and structural expectations of particular com-
munities. While existing writing guides offer general advice, they
are often too abstract and high-level, making it challenging for
junior researchers to apply this guidance in their own work.
Given that people commonly learn through examples, providing
access to relevant examples can help bridge this gap. However, there
are obstacles: viewing too few examples may lead to overfitting
and unintentional plagiarism, while viewing too many examples—
without sufficient cognitive supports within the interface—may
overwhelm the writer.

paragraphs.tag: How does prior work address this with cognitive apprenticeship theory?
paragraphs.text:
Prior work motivated the design of writing support tools with
social cognitive theories and cognitive apprenticeship theory [18,
19] to help writers learn complex writing skills in a professional
setting. While this approach allows novices to learn by mimicking
model examples, it also requires expert knowledge to create and
annotate these examples, which is often time-consuming and not
readily available for many communities.

paragraphs.tag: How has language learning research approached learning from examples?
paragraphs.text:
Learning from examples has also been extensively covered in the
language learning literature. Non-native English speakers (NNES)
may hesitate to choose from AI-suggested content because they
struggle to evaluate the content’s fluency and naturalness [21, 24,
25]. To address this problem, researchers proposed that novices
learn by inspecting sentences from a curated corpus such as the
Corpus of Contemporary American English (COCA)1 or English
dictionaries [4] to help students learn the correct use of colloca-
tions and phrases [35]. To this end, LangSmith proposed a writing
support tool for drafting academic NLP papers [20] by generating
grammatically correct phrases given the user’s current draft along
1https://www.english-corpora.org – accessed 12.09.2024
Hai Dang, Chelse Swoopes, Daniel Buschek, and Elena L. Glassman
with prior section and paper titles. In contrast, our work surfaces ex-
isting text from a relevant peer-reviewed text corpus. Furthermore,
by avoiding automatically generated text that may—without the
writer’s knowledge—cross the line into plagiarism if used verbatim,
the writer only sees previously published example sentences and
their provenance, retaining informed control.

paragraphs.tag: What system was built to address these gaps?
paragraphs.text:
To this end, we implemented CorpusStudio, a writing environ-
ment with two novel writing support concepts, one at the document
level and one at the sentence level, that help writers learn about
the writing styles and expectations of particular audiences. These
writing supports are designed to expose writers to as many ex-
amples as possible to increase the variety of examples shown to
the users—with the cognitive support necessary to help them see
the emergent patterns that capture otherwise implicit community-
specific writing content and style expectations. Specifically, at the
document level, CorpusStudio computes and renders an ordered dis-
tribution [15] over section title sequences in prior papers from the
community the writer wishes to write for. This gives the writer a
sense of common and uncommon section titles and in what relative
order they appear in prior papers (Figure 1A). At the sentence level,
CorpusStudio retrieves many example sentences from the corpus
given the user’s draft-in-progress and their current cursor location
within it (Figure 1C). Words across these many example sentences
are algorithmically highlighted or de-emphasized to help users see
any emergent norms and outliers. We also allow authors to capture
their thoughts and deductions from viewing these examples with
bookmarks and notes.

paragraphs.tag: How was the system evaluated?
paragraphs.text:
We conducted a user study with N=16 participants from the
academic community who were actively writing their manuscripts.
They used CorpusStudio to draft their paper outline, wrote one
to two sections of their manuscript, and answered questionnaires
eliciting their overall experience writing within CorpusStudio.

paragraphs.tag: What did the study find?
paragraphs.text:
Our results reveal that users felt more confident in their writing
when they discovered that other people in their target community
have written in a similar way. Inspecting many examples at once
was useful for identifying broad structural patterns, especially for
sections that typically have more common structure, such as the
description of the system implementation details or participants’
demographics.

In summary, we contribute the following:
•
We designed two novel writing support concepts that make

We implemented these writing support concepts within Cor-
pusStudio, an interactive writing environment that helps

paragraphs.tag: What does this section cover?
paragraphs.text:
In this section we provide a background on writing norms in differ-
ent communities and how members learn about these norms. We
then give an overview of interactive tools that support writing and
tools for finding related work.

2.1 Community Writing Norms
Flower [12]
2.1.1 The Importance of Understanding Writing Norms.

paragraphs.tag: Why does writing for a community's audience matter?
paragraphs.text:
highlights the difference between writer-based and reader-based
prose, arguing that the former represents the writers’ unrefined
thoughts while the latter requires their careful transformation with
the reader goals in mind while ensuring a shared language and
shared context. Prior writing literature emphasizes the importance
of writing for an audience [1, 16, 45], but writing for academic
or professional communities can be especially difficult because
they have implicit writing expectations and failing to address them
may confuse its members or waste their time with “unfocused and
pointless discussions” [12].
2.1.2 Aspects of Writing Norms.

paragraphs.tag: What makes up a community's writing norms?
paragraphs.text:
Writing norms are comprised of
many aspects, including the language, content, organization of
information, and scope of the written document. Although aca-
demic venues may provide a high-level overview of the expected
content and style of writing such as encouraging authors to write
“clearly and concisely, avoid jargon, organize the submission to
detail”2,
flow logically and smoothly, provide the right level of it
can be challenging for novice writers to apply these suggestions in
their own writing, e.g., What is the expected level of detail for that
audience?
2.1.3 Learning about a Community’s Writing Norms.

paragraphs.tag: How do novices learn a community's writing norms?
paragraphs.text:
To support
writing in an academic context, prior research has proposed the
cognitive apprenticeship theoretic approach to teach novices com-
plex cognitive tasks by mimicking experienced members of the
community [8]. Drawing from these ideas, our work instantiates
two strategies of cognitive apprenticeship, namely modeling and
reflection.
2.2 Writing with External Text
2.2.1 Writing with Retrieved or Generated Additional Text.

paragraphs.tag: How do existing tools support writing with external/generated text?
paragraphs.text:
Many
writing support tools facilitate writing by suggesting content that
users did not write themselves. Sentence completions are a frequent
form of writing assistance [2, 28]. However, direct content genera-
tion can have negative impacts such as diminishing the author’s self-
expression and ownership over the final text outcome [30]. Related
work has also looked into providing writing inspirations [6, 14, 43].
We build on this line of research by surfacing prior text as the
user writes new text (e.g., Naeem et al. [37] and IntroAssist [18]). A
critical difference is the much larger scale of prior text surfaced to
the user and post-processed for emergent patterns in our work. For
example, IntroAssist [18] presents expert-curated email examples to
help users draft their help-seeking message in a professional con-
text, while our approach uses computational methods to show many
examples drawn from a large text corpus of previously published
papers.
2.2.2 Writing with Text from a Corpus.

paragraphs.tag: How have prior tools used corpus-based text examples for writing?
paragraphs.text:
Hui and Sprouse [19] pro-
posed a writing support tool to help college students write in a
professional context assisted by scaffolded annotations. The authors
proposed a checklist with multiple annotations that provide cues
about the content to include in the professional email. This checklist

cessed: 31 January 2025
CHI ’25, April 26–May 01, 2025, Yokohama, Japan
is complemented with model texts where sections of that text have
been annotated with the elements of the checklist. This approach
helps users understand the overall structure and expected content
while also demonstrating concrete instantiations of the high-level
guidelines. Our concepts help users plan the structure and content
of their writing by showing many concrete examples of how other
members of their target community have written similar texts.
2.3 Finding Relevant Examples

paragraphs.tag: Why is finding relevant writing examples via search hard?
paragraphs.text:
As previously described, writers learn from inspecting examples,
but finding related work with the purpose of writing support is chal-
lenging. Search engines such as Google Scholar, the ACM Digital
Library, Mendeley, and Semantic Scholar typically surface docu-
ments based on topical similarity while writers need specific analo-
gous snippets of text from the manuscript to inform their writing.

paragraphs.tag: How do current tools help relate one's work to others'?
paragraphs.text:
Current tools also help researchers understand how their own
work relates to other work [29] by contextualizing embedded cita-
tions [5], drawing connections to follow-on work directly in the
paper document [40], and making recommendations based on a
paper’s metadata such as citations and authorship [7, 23, 39, 42] or
its semantic similarity [3, 17, 23]. In contrast, our design focuses on
finding related work for the purpose of writing support, i.e., that
helps writers identify existing writing conventions from a specific
community.

paragraphs.tag: What gap exists in integrating writing and related-work search?
paragraphs.text:
Most interactive research tools either support analyzing related
work [26, 29, 33, 38] or writing with computational help [9, 28]. In
existing contexts, writers often need to navigate away from their
writing environment to search for related work, scroll through the
target document, select and process relevant text structures and
draw conclusions about the implicit writing conventions encoded
in the target document. Performing all of these steps leads to abrupt
context switches and breaks the writing flow. Our approach pro-
poses an integrated environment to support writing and searching
for model text in the same interface, thereby minimizing the num-
ber of context switches and streamlining the writing and research
process.

paragraphs.tag: What is CorpusStudio's main design purpose?
paragraphs.text:
We designed CorpusStudio to support writers in learning about
and applying community-specific writing norms. This is achieved
primarily through novel mechanisms for the retrieval and rendering
of content from a corpus of existing documents written by and for
that community.
3.1 Design Goals

paragraphs.tag: What are the overarching design goals?
paragraphs.text:
Our overarching design goal is to empower users with evidence of
community-specific emergent norms and outliers at the document
and sentence level as they write their own document for the same
audience. In the process of fulfilling this overarching goal, our goal
is to reduce, not facilitate, unintentional human- or AI-generated
plagiarism.
3.2 Usage Scenario

paragraphs.tag: How does a user first explore the system?
paragraphs.text:
Alice has been working on a new interactive writing support system
and is drafting her manuscript for submission to an HCI venue. She
has some prior experience writing academic papers but is unfamiliar

CHI ’25, April 26–May 01, 2025, Yokohama, Japan
with writing papers with a focus on a system contribution. She
opens CorpusStudio to learn more about her target venue’s writing
expectations while working on her draft.

paragraphs.tag: How does the user inspect section titles?
paragraphs.text:
Inspecting the section titles. She looks at the ordered distribution
over section titles. As shown in Figure 1A, she expands the cluster
named Implementation, which typically comes after System Design
and around the same location as Methods (when those sections
exist in a given paper). In the expanded cluster, she observes how
other authors have phrased this typical section’s title, i.e., more
commonly Implementation and less commonly Implementation De-
tails or Implementation of <System Name>. Although she likes the
idea of adding a system name to the title, she decides to stick with
the more generic commonly chosen option for now, and finishes
her paper outline of section titles in the text editor beside it.

paragraphs.tag: How does the user retrieve example sentences?
paragraphs.text:
Inspecting the retrieved sentences. In the text editor, she starts
drafting the implementation section immediately under the Im-
plementation section title, but she does not know how she should
introduce it. She writes a few words and, without moving the cursor,
hits the TAB key to retrieve related sentences from other work to
get a sense of what (and how) other people wrote the beginnings of
their implementation sections. She notices that many authors start
with “We implemented <name of the system> to do/test <some
hypothesis>” while some also state their design rationale.

paragraphs.tag: How does the user build a personal style sheet?
paragraphs.text:
Developing a personal style sheet. She bookmarks one of the re-
trieved sentences to remind herself of this observation and adds the
note: “The first paragraph of the implementation is often formulaic
and with this recognizable structure.” She concludes that it is prob-
ably well accepted in the community if she starts her paragraph in
a similar way.

paragraphs.tag: How does the user continue using the system while writing?
paragraphs.text:
Continuing Writing. Alice continues to write down her ideas in
the text editor and occasionally retrieves example sentences given Introduction is the ubiquitous starting
where her cursor is when she needs inspiration or wants to confirm
how other authors have written their manuscripts.
3.3 System Characteristics

paragraphs.tag: What theoretical basis informs the system's design?
paragraphs.text:
In this work, the evidence of community-specific emergent norms
and outliers at both the document and sentence level is provided
to writers in the form of extracted examples from a corpus of doc-
uments written for and by their intended audience. To facilitate
the writer’s recognition of these emergent norms from examples
without facilitating the writer’s anchoring on any one example too
much, we look to theories of human concept learning:

paragraphs.tag: What is Variation Theory and how does it inform design?
paragraphs.text:
Variation Theory. Regardless of whether a human or a machine
is learning from examples, any learning process can fall victim to
overfitting, i.e., learn a rule that does not generalize to the rest of the
corpus, when trained on too little data. For example, the Variation
Theory of Learning [32] was explicitly designed to minimize human
overfitting when learning from examples. With only a few examples
or suggestions, previous systems may cause users to anchor [46] on
just one of them. By instead showing many examples, we hope the
user may be (1) less likely to anchor to one of the retrieved examples
(or even unintentionally plagiarize from it) and (2) more likely
to observe community writing norms and possibilities without
overfitting to the retrieved examples.
Hai Dang, Chelse Swoopes, Daniel Buschek, and Elena L. Glassman

paragraphs.tag: What is Structural Alignment Theory and how does it inform rendering?
paragraphs.text:
Structural Alignment Theory. While the many retrieved examples
in our work are not algorithmically selected on the basis of Variation
Theory, the textual examples are ordered and rendered with visual
attributes (e.g., grayed-out repeated words or color-coordinated
highlights) designed to support the recognition of emergent com-
monalities and outliers, based on the human cognitive processes of
pattern recognition described by Structural Alignment Theory [13].

paragraphs.tag: What is the central text editor's design?
paragraphs.text:
3.3.1 Text Editor. Users outline their paper and draft their prose
in the central text editor (Figure 1B). The editor supports two text
cell types: section title and paragraph.

paragraphs.tag: How is section title syntax created?
paragraphs.text:
Borrowing from the syntax of Markdown editors, the editor
allows users to create section titles by pre-pending text with #’s
where the number of #’s indicate the level of the section title.

paragraphs.tag: How does the system surface document-level norms?
paragraphs.text:
3.3.2 Surfacing Document-levelCommunity-specificEmergentNorms
and Outliers. Inspecting outlines from other papers in the target
community can help writers develop their own. To help writers un-
derstand how papers are commonly (and uncommonly) structured
within their target community at the document level, we show an
ordered distribution of section title clusters from the entire corpus
immediately to the left of the central text editor (Figure 1A Section
Titles From Other Papers). This ordered distribution is computed by
applying Positional Diction Clustering (PDC) [15] to the ordered
lists of top-level section titles extracted from each paper in the
corpus.

paragraphs.tag: How does PDC algorithm work to order section titles?
paragraphs.text:
PDC is a structural mapping engine [11] designed to algorith-
mically emulate at scale the analogical matching process humans
do when comparing two or more structurally similar objects, as de-
scribed by Structural Alignment Theory [13]. In CorpusStudio, the
objects are papers, and the resulting order of section title clusters
that PDC generates preserves the section titles’ approximate rela-
tive positions in their respective papers. For example, in Figure 1A,

paragraphs.tag: How are section title clusters visually presented?

Section title clusters are shown with a count and a proportion-

paragraphs.tag: How does the interface highlight commonalities and variations in clusters?

We also provide cognitive support for perceiving the common-

about the cluster contents when it is closed. Within each cluster,
the PDC algorithm dictates the order of section titles to minimize
diction differences between section titles in adjacent rows; words
that appeared previously in the ordered list of cluster members
are greyed out so that variations might be more visible. This text
graying strategy is based on the interleaved view of PDC results in
Gero et al. [15].

paragraphs.tag: How does the system surface sentence-level norms?

3.3.3 Surfacing Sentence-level Community-specific Emergent Norms
and Outliers. This writing support is intended to provide insights
into both established conventions and areas where variation is
common at the sentence level. By retrieving and displaying many
relevant sentences simultaneously, users can observe how similar
content is expressed across different papers. These distributions can
reveal both rigid conventions (narrow distributions) and areas of
flexibility (wide distributions). For instance, participant descriptions
in user studies often follow stereotypical patterns, while discus-
sion sections typically show more variation to accommodate novel
findings.

paragraphs.tag: What is the spatial retrieval mechanism?
paragraphs.text:
Spatial Retrieval. At the core of our approach is a novel retrieval
mechanism we call analogous spatial retrieval, which integrates
context, content, and spatial information. Users can request this
retrieval of sentences from other papers by hitting the TAB key
as they are drafting their text. Given where the user’s cursor is
placed in the text editor at the moment of retrieval (i.e., the text
of the currently focused paragraph cell and the title of the section
containing it), we retrieve and display many potentially analogous
sentences from similarly titled sections of papers in the corpus
(Figure 1C What others wrote column) as well as the subsequent
sentence in each paper (Figure 1C What they wrote next column). See
Section 3.4 and Section 4.2 for more spatial retrieval implementation
details.

paragraphs.tag: How can users preview future content via offset retrieval?
paragraphs.text:
To further help writers “peek into the future,” that is, explore
what other authors wrote later in a given section, users can insert
empty paragraph cells after a non-empty paragraph cell and then
trigger sentence retrieval. The number of empty cells corresponds
to the offset o (in sentences) to be retrieved from the corpus. Retriev-
ing content with an offset works by first retrieving all sentences
that would have been retrieved if the cursor had been in the near-
est preceding non-empty paragraph cell but then retrieving and
displaying the o-th subsequent sentences.

paragraphs.tag: How was the number of retrieved sentences determined?
paragraphs.text:
Scale of Retrieval. Following Gentner’s work on analogical learn-
ing theory [13], the comparison of many example sentences pro-
motes the extraction of common principles or abstract schemas,
which may be more likely to be transferred to future writing tasks.
We experimented with displaying 10, 25 and 50 sentences at once
and found that 25 sentences provided enough content for writers to
explore and potentially recognize common principles and abstract
schemas while not overwhelming them.

examples depends not only on their scale and variety, but also on
how the writer mentally processes and compares them [13]. To aid
in this mental sentence comparison process, the sentence examples
can be rendered with algorithmically assigned visual variables (e.g.,
color-coordinated highlights) designed to support the recognition
of emergent commonalities and outliers (and possibly support the
mental cross-sentence alignment process necessary for developing
abstract sentence schemas). Figure 2 shows a comparison of the

paragraphs.tag: How does re-ranking let users explore relationships?
paragraphs.text:
Re-ranking is another way for users to explore relationships
across sentences. When users click on the re-ranking icon (arrow
below bookmark icon next to each sentence), the selected sentence
moves to the top of its column in Figure 1C. CorpusStudio then sorts
the other sentences in ascending cosine-distance from that new
top sentence. This triggers the system to recompute the greyed-out
words to account for the new sorted column.

fulfills its purpose particularly well or poorly. These annotated
sentence examples can be exported as a csv file to facilitate sharing

paragraphs.tag: What are contextual tooltips for?
paragraphs.text:
3.3.5 Contextual Tooltips. Writers may want to know more of the
context surrounding a retrieved sentence, e.g., to avoid misinter-
preting it. As shown in Figure 1D, users can hover over a retrieved
sentence to view a floating window showing the paper’s title, the
hierarchical section title path, and the sentences immediately before
and after. The paper title links to the full paper in the ACM Digital
Library. Additionally, if any retrieved sentence includes a citation,
users can hover over it to display the full citation information,
including the authors and the referenced paper title.

paragraphs.tag: How do design features promote learning over plagiarism?
paragraphs.text:
3.3.6 Features for Promoting Learning, not Plagiarism. A combina-
tion of features are intended to work together to support users in
actively engaging with many examples, rather than anchoring on
and copying any one. More specifically, showing multiple examples
at once may help novice writers make more informed decisions
about plagiarism: when sentences are highly similar across papers,
this often indicates accepted community writing norms (like in
methodology sections), while sections with more varied writing
styles suggest areas where similar phrasing should be avoided.

paragraphs.tag: What additional design choices discourage plagiarism?
paragraphs.text:
In concert with showing many examples, two additional design
choices are intended to further facilitate learning over plagiarism:
First, we disable the user’s ability to copy and paste retrieved sen-
tences into their own draft. Second, by providing visible affordances
for saving and annotating their insights, we may promote deeper
reflection on the writing patterns they observe.
3.4 Implementation Details

paragraphs.tag: What technology stack was used to implement the system?
paragraphs.text:
SvelteKit.4
We implemented our system as a web application using
WeaviateDB5
For sentence retrieval, we used as our vector database,
using its built-in text embedding capabilities and approximate k-

was deployed on a workstation with 12 GB of GPU memory and
made remotely accessible to study participants.

paragraphs.tag: Why was vector-based search chosen over hybrid search?
paragraphs.text:
While determining relevance in retrieval systems is inherently
complex and depends on users’ dynamic writing objectives, query-
ing based on semantic similarity in text vector space is an estab-
lished approach in retrieval-based systems [47]. Our initial im-
plementation explored hybrid search techniques, following prior
work that used Reciprocal Rank Fusion [41] to combine keyword-
based and vector-based retrieval results. However, through initial
experiments, we found pure vector-based search provided more
contextually relevant matches.

paragraphs.tag: What corpus was collected?
paragraphs.text:
We collected 478 papers from two HCI venues (IUI and UIST) which
included the proceedings from 2021 until 2023. These venues typ-
ically publish HCI system contributions. We completed the data
request process with the ACM.
4.1 Pre-processing Documents

paragraphs.tag: How were documents split into sentences?
paragraphs.text:
We initially used the NLTK module to split each manuscript into
sentences, but we experienced many edge cases where extracted
sentences were incomplete. We therefore chose an LLM-based ap-
proach instructing the model to separate sentences by inserting

4.2 Embedding Process

paragraphs.tag: How were sentences embedded for retrieval?
paragraphs.text:
To implement spatial retrieval, we follow an approach resembling
LangSmith [20]. We prepared our corpus to support this function-
ality by pre-pending section titles to the extracted sentences be-
fore embedding the concatenated sequence using OpenAI’s ‘text-
embedding-small-3‘ model (Figure 4). This approach enables Cor-
pusStudio to retrieve related sentences based on both the section
title and the content of the sentence. We used default parameter
values and default un-trimmed vector dimensions.
4.3 Extracting an Ordered Distribution over
Section Titles

paragraphs.tag: How was section title structure extracted and clustered?
paragraphs.text:
The sequences of top-level section titles for each paper were ex-
tracted and organized into a list of lists using positional diction
clustering (PDC) [15]. This is identical to the process that produced
the data for the Interleaved PDC view in Gero et al. [15], except
instead of processing LLM responses as sequences of sentences,
we processed papers as sequences of section titles. We also com-
puted how many papers had each section title in order to populate
a corresponding histogram in the CorpusStudio interface.

paragraphs.tag: What sample size was chosen and why?
paragraphs.text:
We experimented with different sample sizes ranging from 200,
500, 1000, to 5000 section titles and found that distinctive distribu-
tion characteristics quickly emerged even with smaller sample sizes.
For our prototype we decided to render and cluster 1000 section
titles to demonstrate both the defining characteristics of the section
title distribution while still providing a variety of ways authors
have organized and phrased their section titles.

paragraphs.tag: What is the goal and design of the user study?
paragraphs.text:
To evaluate our two novel writing support concepts (described
at the document level in Section 3.3.2 and at the sentence level
in Section 3.3.3), we used CorpusStudio to conduct a controlled
within-subjects experiment with participants who were, with one
exception, actively working towards writing a manuscript for an
HCI venue. Participants completed two writing tasks during the
user study: (i) drafting or revising an outline of their paper and (ii)
drafting or revising section(s) of their paper. We referred to Cor-
pusStudio as a “set of design features” or “prototype” during our
user evaluation of the concepts. We used Google Docs as our base-
line interface because it is a commonly used writing environment
in this context. We aimed to investigate how participants would
use the writing supports to achieve their goals, how the supports
would affect their writing process, and how they may help them
identify norms of a target community.

8.1 Relevance of Retrieved Sentences
We found that relevance of retrieved sentences was tightly coupled
with users’ writing intentions, as they found different uses and
rationales for integrating the retrieved results into their writing
process.
8.1.1 Users’ Diverse Applications of Retrieved Sentences. While Cor-
pusStudio uses text embeddings to capture semantic and syntactic
relationships [36], our study revealed that relevance was also deter-
mined by participants’ writing goals rather than semantic similarity
alone. For instance, semantically similar sentences were sometimes
less useful than structurally similar ones when writers sought to
understand the organization of the paper.
Participants sought inspiration at multiple levels of writing: from
paper organization through section titles to section-level transitions
and standard academic phrases. The writers shaped these results
through queries using their draft text itself, similar to patterns ob-
served in interactions with AI in writing [10]. This challenges funda-
mental information retrieval assumptions about query-document
similarity as an (only) indicator of relevance. While it provided
a useful starting point, our findings suggest that relevance of re-
trieved text in writing support systems is not fixed, but dynamically
constructed based on writers’ immediate goals.
8.1.2 Interpreting Retrieved Results: User Behaviors and Dataset
Limitations. Our study revealed how retrieved examples influenced
participants’ writing in unexpected ways. When participants were
looking for something specific and did not find it in the retrieved
results, this led to two notable behaviors: First, participants often
rephrased their text to get different results, blurring the line be-
tween writing and querying. Second, some interpreted a lack of
results as evidence of their work’s novelty, a problematic conclusion
given CorpusStudio’s limited scope (two HCI venues: IUI and UIST
from 2021-2023). These findings suggest that writing support sys-
tems should actively communicate their scope and limitations, for
instance by suggesting broader venue searches when topic-specific
queries yield no results, helping writers make informed decisions
about how to interpret search results.
